new_slides.title: A single LG spike is enough to command a tail flip
body: A **command neuron** is one whose activity is both necessary and sufficient for a particular behavior: blocking it prevents the act, and activating it alone produces the act. The lateral giant meets both tests for its tail flip, since a single LG spike is enough to produce the stereotyped flexion that throws the crayfish away from a stimulus at its rear.

One spike suffices because the output is built for reliability. Each giant drives the motor giant through a direct electrical synapse and the segmental giant, which in turn excites the fast-flexor motor neurons, so one impulse reaches the abdominal flexor muscles of every segment within milliseconds.

The decision to fire is less centralized than the term suggests. Whether LG reaches threshold depends on sensory afferents, interneurons and their interactions with LG's own dendrites, so the command neuron is the final common point of a distributed decision.

figure.caption: Wine & Krasne (1972), Fig. 2. Simultaneous connective and abdominal recordings of giant-fiber activity.

new_slides.cite: Wine & Krasne (1972); Herberholz et al. (2002); Fraser & Heitler (1991)
transcript: Slide 3 identifies LG and MG activity from implanted electrodes; the significance of identifying a single giant spike comes from the command-neuron concept, which the later cellular studies refine.
Necessity and sufficiency define a command neuron.
Herberholz and colleagues describe a single LG spike as necessary and sufficient to produce a highly stereotyped tail flip that thrusts the animal away from the source of stimulation.
That makes an extracellularly recorded giant spike, as on slide 3, a reliable marker of which escape pathway produced the movement.
The output side guarantees that one spike is enough.

Fraser and Heitler describe each giant fiber driving the motor giant through a monosynaptic electrical connection, while the remaining fast-flexor motor neurons receive most of their input through the segmental giant.
Electrical synapses transmit with almost no delay, consistent with the roughly two-millisecond interval between giant spikes and abdominal muscle potentials.
The input side spreads the decision across many cells.
Herberholz and colleagues conclude that the decision to escape depends on interactions between LG's dendritic potentials and the primary afferent terminals in a lateral excitatory network.
LG is therefore the point at which the decision becomes all-or-none, not the only place where it is computed.
refs: J. J. Wine; F. B. Krasne (1972). The Organization of Escape Behaviour in the Crayfish. Journal of Experimental Biology 56(1):1–18. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.56.1.1

J. Herberholz; B. L. Antonsen; D. H. Edwards (2002). A lateral excitatory network in the escape circuit of crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 22(20):9078–9085. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-20-09078.2002

K. Fraser; W. J. Heitler (1991). Photoinactivation of the crayfish segmental giant neuron reveals a direct giant-fiber to fast-flexor connection with a chemical component. Journal of Neuroscience 11(1):59–71. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-01-00059.1991

new_slides.title: Giant circuits trade sensory guidance for speed
body: Giant-mediated tail flips start within milliseconds but follow a trajectory fixed by which giant fired, leaving little room for sensory guidance. Nongiant flips start later but can be steered, truncated or redirected, since the extra time allows sensory information to shape the movement.

The nervous system must therefore choose which system to use almost as soon as a stimulus begins. Vu and colleagues propose abruptness as the criterion: only stimuli that rise steeply enough to excite LG to threshold within a few milliseconds trigger the giant response, while slower stimuli fall to the nongiant system.
The criterion plausibly matches the risk. An abrupt touch, such as a sudden strike, leaves no time for a guided response, whereas a slowly building stimulus allows the slower, more flexible escape.

figure.caption: Wine & Krasne (1972), Fig. 3(A,B). Giant-mediated initial responses followed by nongiant swimming.

transcript: Slides 2 to 6 describe two families of tail flip with different speeds and different flexibility; the reason both exist is that speed and guidance cannot be maximized together.
Speed limits guidance.
A giant-mediated flip is triggered by one spike and runs its course in a fixed form, so there is no time for sensory information to adjust it.
Nongiant flips, with their longer latencies, can incorporate information about the surroundings, which is why they include truncated flips and changes of direction.
The choice has to be made fast.
Vu and colleagues frame the problem as a rapid assessment of whether to use the fast reflex system or the slower nongiant one.
Their answer is that only stimuli strong enough to fire LG before postexcitatory inhibition begins, within a few milliseconds, recruit the giant system.
The behavioral data fit this rule.
On slide 4, abrupt taps usually recruited giant activity while gradually rising pinches of similar effectiveness did not.
The cellular mechanisms that implement the rule appear later in the deck, in the coincidence detection and inhibition experiments.
refs: J. J. Wine; F. B. Krasne (1972). The Organization of Escape Behaviour in the Crayfish. Journal of Experimental Biology 56(1):1–18. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.56.1.1

E. T. Vu; A. Berkowitz; F. B. Krasne (1997). Postexcitatory inhibition of the crayfish lateral giant neuron: a mechanism for sensory temporal filtering. Journal of Neuroscience 17(22):8867–8879. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.17-22-08867.1997

new_slides.title: Gap junctions pass both current and small molecules
body: An **electrical synapse** is formed by gap junctions, clusters of channels that connect the cytoplasm of two neurons directly. Current flows through them without transmitter release, so a voltage change in one cell appears in the other with essentially no synaptic delay.

The same channels have pores wide enough for small molecules but not large ones. The two-tracer method exploits that size limit: small Neurobiotin crosses into coupled partners, while the large dextran conjugate stays in the injected cell, so labeled partners identify cells joined by open junctions.

Electrical coupling suits an escape circuit. It is fast, it allows many inputs to combine onto LG with little delay, and coupled cells can recruit one another. Its voltage dependence adds a timing selectivity that a simple conductive link would lack.

figure.caption: Herberholz et al. (2002), Fig. 2(A). LG and dye-coupled neurons in the terminal ganglion.

new_slides.cite: Herberholz et al. (2002); Edwards et al. (1991)
transcript: Slide 11 uses two tracers of different size to separate LG from its coupled partners; the logic depends on what a gap junction is.
Gap junctions are channels between cells.
Each junction aligns channels in the two membranes so that ions, and molecules below a size limit, pass directly from one cytoplasm to the other.
Since no transmitter must be released and bind receptors, the electrical signal crosses immediately.
Tracer size turns this into a labeling method.
A tracer small enough to pass the junctions spreads from the injected cell into every cell coupled to it.
A tracer too large to pass marks only the injected cell, so cells labeled by the small tracer alone are the coupled partners.
The escape circuit uses this coupling extensively.
Edwards and colleagues describe a massive convergence of mechanosensory inputs onto LG through electrical synapses from both afferents and interneurons.
Dye coupling establishes that the pathway exists; the paired recordings on slide 14 establish that it transmits electrical signals.
refs: J. Herberholz; B. L. Antonsen; D. H. Edwards (2002). A lateral excitatory network in the escape circuit of crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 22(20):9078–9085. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-20-09078.2002

D. H. Edwards; W. J. Heitler; E. M. Leise; R. A. Fricke (1991). Postsynaptic modulation of rectifying electrical synaptic inputs to the LG escape command neuron in crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 11(7):2117–2129. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-07-02117.1991

new_slides.title: Lateral excitation makes LG recruitment self-reinforcing
body: The afferent network works as **positive feedback**. A stimulated afferent excites coupled neighbors, recruited neighbors add input to LG and to interneurons, and LG depolarization spreads back to bring further afferents and interneurons to threshold. Each step increases the excitation that drives the following one.

Herberholz and colleagues describe the result as nonlinear amplification: below a critical level of input little is recruited, but once recruitment starts it grows rapidly. The circuit can thereby convert a graded mechanical stimulus into a sharp threshold for escape.

This moves part of the decision out of LG itself. Whether the crayfish escapes depends on interactions between LG's dendritic potentials and the afferent terminals, not only on summation within LG, which is why identical shocks gave different outcomes when LG voltage was shifted.

figure.caption: Herberholz et al. (2002), Fig. 4(A,B). Increasing nerve shocks recruit sensory EPSPs and afferent spikes.

transcript: Slides 13 to 18 build up the lateral excitatory network one observation at a time; taken together, they describe a positive feedback loop.
Each element of the loop was measured separately.

Afferents are coupled to each other on slides 13 and 14, stronger shocks recruit afferents that were not directly stimulated on slide 15, and LG voltage changes the recruitment of afferents and interneurons on slides 16 to 18.
Combined, these mean that excitation in any part of the network increases excitation in the other parts.
Positive feedback produces a threshold.
With weak input, recruitment stays small and the loop does not take off.
Once input is strong enough to recruit additional afferents, the added input recruits still more, so the response grows disproportionately; the authors call this nonlinear amplification.
The network also links to the abruptness rule.
An abrupt stimulus that excites many afferents together is the one most likely to start this self-reinforcing recruitment.
Hyperpolarizing LG, by contrast, reduced the excitability of afferents and interneurons, showing that the loop can also be damped.
refs: J. Herberholz; B. L. Antonsen; D. H. Edwards (2002). A lateral excitatory network in the escape circuit of crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 22(20):9078–9085. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-20-09078.2002

new_slides.title: Rectifying junctions weaken inputs after LG depolarizes
body: A **rectifying** electrical synapse passes current readily in one direction, from a presynaptic cell more depolarized than its target, and poorly in the other, much as an electrical diode does. It opens when the presynaptic side is depolarized relative to the postsynaptic side.

Once earlier inputs depolarize LG, that difference shrinks, the junction is **reverse-biased**, and later inputs pass less current. Edwards and colleagues propose that this raises LG's relative sensitivity to novel, abrupt stimuli: a fresh volley reaching a resting LG is transmitted strongly, while input trailing an ongoing response is discounted.

The same property explains why reverse transfer is limited but not absent: hyperpolarizing LG drives current back into interneuron A more readily than depolarizing it does. Rectification shapes the circuit's timing preference without isolating its cells from one another.

figure.caption: Edwards et al. (1991), Fig. 3(A–D). Interneuron A transmission and voltage-dependent LG responses.

transcript: Slides 20 and 21 establish that the connection from interneuron A to LG depends on LG's voltage; the diode comparison makes the direction of that dependence intuitive.
Rectification follows the voltage difference.
The junction opens when the presynaptic side is depolarized relative to the postsynaptic side, so current flows from interneuron to LG during an input spike.
Hyperpolarizing LG enlarges the difference and the input; depolarizing LG shrinks it, which is the pattern recorded on slide 20.
Reverse bias has a functional consequence.
Edwards and colleagues describe postsynaptic depolarization produced by earlier inputs as reverse-biasing the rectifying input synapses and reducing their strength.
LG is therefore most sensitive to input that arrives while it is at rest, which favors novel, phasic stimuli over continuing ones.
Two results that look contradictory concern different measurements.
Depolarizing LG reduces a fixed unitary input on slide 20 yet increases total input through network recruitment on slide 19.
One measures a single connection, the other the number of active inputs, so both can hold at once.
refs: D. H. Edwards; W. J. Heitler; E. M. Leise; R. A. Fricke (1991). Postsynaptic modulation of rectifying electrical synaptic inputs to the LG escape command neuron in crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 11(7):2117–2129. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-07-02117.1991

new_slides.title: Shunting inhibition opens a leak that excitation must fill
body: Chloride channels whose reversal potential lies near the resting voltage change the voltage little when they open. They raise membrane conductance, however, so excitatory current arriving at the same time leaks out through them and produces a smaller EPSP: the inhibition scales excitation down instead of subtracting a fixed amount.

Shunting acts mainly near the open channels. Inhibition directed to LG's distal dendrites therefore suppresses input arriving on those branches more than input elsewhere, consistent with stronger attenuation for a repeated shock to the same root than to a different root.

Arriving a few milliseconds after excitation, this inhibition closes a window. Excitation that reaches threshold before the shunt develops triggers the escape; excitation still building when it arrives is curtailed.

figure.caption: Vu et al. (1997), Fig. 6(A,B). Reduced attenuation of injected-current responses during picrotoxin.

transcript: Slides 27 to 30 measure postexcitatory inhibition as reduced EPSPs, reduced input resistance and partial spatial specificity; the shunting mechanism ties these together.
Shunting is a conductance effect.
The size of a voltage change produced by a current depends on how easily current can leave the cell; opening extra channels allows it to leave more easily.
That is why Vu and colleagues measured input resistance on slide 29: a drop in resistance during the late response is the signature of opened channels, whatever their effect on resting voltage.
Location gives the inhibition specificity.
Vu and colleagues report that postexcitatory inhibition is directed to distal LG dendrites, allowing some location specificity within the sensory field of one hemisegment.
A shunt near one dendritic branch mainly affects input arriving on that branch, as the same-root versus different-root comparison on slide 30 suggests.
The timing of the shunt matters most for behavior.
Inhibition that begins a few milliseconds after stimulus onset leaves only a short window in which LG can reach threshold.
Only rapidly rising stimuli succeed within that window, which links this cellular mechanism to the abruptness rule for giant escape.
refs: E. T. Vu; A. Berkowitz; F. B. Krasne (1997). Postexcitatory inhibition of the crayfish lateral giant neuron: a mechanism for sensory temporal filtering. Journal of Neuroscience 17(22):8867–8879. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.17-22-08867.1997

new_slides.title: Three timing filters let only abrupt stimuli fire LG
body: Taps recruited the giants while slowly rising pinches of similar effectiveness did not, and three mechanisms account for this preference. Rectifying junctions sum synchronous afferent input strongly but reduce input arriving even 0.1 ms late, so only a volley in which many afferents fire together produces a large EPSP.

Lateral excitation among afferents then amplifies a strong synchronous volley into rapid recruitment. Within a few milliseconds, postexcitatory inhibition shunts LG's dendrites, so a stimulus that has not driven LG to threshold by then loses its chance.

An abrupt mechanical stimulus excites many hairs at once and passes all three filters; a gradual one recruits afferents over a longer time and fails them, leaving the response to the slower nongiant system. The abruptness rule seen in free animals thus follows from synaptic properties measured in isolated nerve cords.

figure.caption: Edwards et al. (1998), Fig. 3(B). LG EPSP amplitude as a function of sensory-input delay.

new_slides.cite: Wine & Krasne (1972); Edwards et al. (1998); Herberholz et al. (2002); Vu et al. (1997)
transcript: Slide 4 established behaviorally that abrupt stimuli recruit the giants; slides 15 to 30 supply three cellular mechanisms, and together they explain the behavioral rule.
The first filter operates on the scale of microseconds.
Edwards and colleagues found that LG sums synchronous inputs but not inputs separated by only one hundred microseconds.
They state that this coincidence detection enables crayfish to produce reflex escape only to very abrupt mechanical stimuli.
The second filter amplifies what passes the first.
A synchronous volley that depolarizes afferent terminals and LG together recruits additional afferents through the lateral excitatory network.
Asynchronous input produces less depolarization at any moment and so recruits less.
The third filter sets a deadline.
Vu and colleagues found that only stimuli strong enough to fire LG before postexcitatory inhibition begins, within a few milliseconds of onset, trigger giant responses.
The three filters act on different timescales, from tenths of a millisecond to several milliseconds, but all favor the same kind of stimulus.
refs: J. J. Wine; F. B. Krasne (1972). The Organization of Escape Behaviour in the Crayfish. Journal of Experimental Biology 56(1):1–18. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.56.1.1

D. H. Edwards; S.-R. Yeh; F. B. Krasne (1998). Neuronal coincidence detection by voltage-sensitive electrical synapses. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 95(12):7145–7150. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.95.12.7145

E. T. Vu; A. Berkowitz; F. B. Krasne (1997). Postexcitatory inhibition of the crayfish lateral giant neuron: a mechanism for sensory temporal filtering. Journal of Neuroscience 17(22):8867–8879. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.17-22-08867.1997

J. Herberholz; B. L. Antonsen; D. H. Edwards (2002). A lateral excitatory network in the escape circuit of crayfish. Journal of Neuroscience 22(20):9078–9085. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-20-09078.2002

new_slides.title: Light and a dye fill silence only the filled neuron
body: Photoinactivation relies on a dye injected into one identified neuron. Intense light excites the dye, which transfers energy to oxygen and produces reactive molecules that damage nearby membranes and proteins. Damage is confined to the filled cell, so neighbors in the same ganglion are spared although the whole region is illuminated.

Progressive damage is consistent with the stages seen in SG. Spikes broaden as repolarization fails, the cell sits on a long depolarized plateau, and it finally loses electrical responsiveness as membrane function collapses.

The method answers a question that cutting a connective cannot: what remains when one identified relay neuron is removed from an otherwise intact circuit. Its limitation is the plateau stage, when a depolarized SG can still pass current to electrically coupled partners.

figure.caption: Fraser & Heitler (1991), Fig. 1(A–C). Recordings before and during dye-mediated segmental-giant inactivation.

transcript: Slide 31 describes the sequence of changes in SG during illumination; the photochemistry of the method explains both its selectivity and its stages.
Selectivity comes from the dye, not the light.
Every cell in the illuminated field receives light, but only the filled cell contains the dye that converts light into damaging reactive molecules.
This allows one identified neuron to be removed while its neighbors and the rest of the circuit remain functional.
The stages reflect accumulating damage.

Fraser and Heitler describe an initial broadening of the spike, a long-duration, massively depolarized plateau, loss of spike capability, a gradual fall in resting potential and eventual loss of responsiveness.
Only after the final stage can the remaining circuit be treated as lacking SG.
Selective removal differs from the lesions on slide 7.
Cutting the nerve cord removes every signal crossing the cut, so it tests pathway dependence without identifying a cell.
Photoinactivating one relay tests the contribution of that identified neuron, which is what exposed the direct giant-to-flexor connections on slides 32 and 33.
refs: K. Fraser; W. J. Heitler (1991). Photoinactivation of the crayfish segmental giant neuron reveals a direct giant-fiber to fast-flexor connection with a chemical component. Journal of Neuroscience 11(1):59–71. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-01-00059.1991

new_slides.title: Removing a dominant pathway can unmask a hidden one
body: In the intact circuit both giants excite the fast-flexor motor neurons mainly through the shared segmental giant, so any direct connection from a giant to those motor neurons is hidden beneath a much larger relayed response. Removing SG on both sides strips away that shared route and exposes what lies beneath it.

The exposed connections differ: a direct LG input graded from anterior to posterior ganglia, and little MG input. Fraser and Heitler suggest that this direct pathway gives clues to an early evolutionary form of the circuit, onto which the shared relay was later added.

Parallel direct and relayed outputs make the motor command robust. The relay recruits all fast flexors strongly, while the direct LG pathway, with its chemical component, provides an additional, differently timed contribution in anterior segments.

figure.caption: Fraser & Heitler (1991), Fig. 4(A,B). Comparisons of LG and MG input after SG removal.

transcript: Slide 33 compares residual LG and MG outputs after SG removal; the general principle is that a strong pathway can mask weaker parallel ones until it is removed.
Masking is a common problem in circuit analysis.
When two pathways converge on the same target, the larger one can dominate the recorded response so completely that the smaller one is invisible.
Removing the dominant pathway, as photoinactivation of SG did, is a direct way to reveal the hidden contribution.
The unmasked pathways are unequal.
After both relays were gone, LG still excited fast flexors, more strongly toward the front of the abdomen than the rear, whereas MG barely did.
These differences match the distinct movements produced by the two giants, upward pitching for LG and backward darting for MG.
The evolutionary reading is a hypothesis.
Fraser and Heitler describe the differences as clues to a probable early form of the circuit.
Testing that idea would require evidence about ancestral circuits; the measured result is the present-day distribution of residual connections.
refs: K. Fraser; W. J. Heitler (1991). Photoinactivation of the crayfish segmental giant neuron reveals a direct giant-fiber to fast-flexor connection with a chemical component. Journal of Neuroscience 11(1):59–71. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-01-00059.1991

new_slides.title: Chemical synapses slow more on cooling than electrical ones
body: Chemical transmission involves sequential steps: calcium entry into the terminal, vesicle fusion, transmitter diffusion and receptor opening. Each step is a temperature-sensitive biochemical process, so cooling lengthens the delay of a chemical synapse considerably.

Current through a gap junction needs no such steps and crosses with almost no delay at any temperature. Cooling therefore pulls the two components of a mixed connection apart in time, the electrical one staying locked to the presynaptic spike and the chemical one falling behind.

Cadmium blocks the calcium channels that trigger release while leaving gap junctions conducting, which is why obligatory electrical giant-to-motor-giant transmission survived it. A component that both lags on cooling and disappears with cadmium carries both signatures of a chemical synapse.

figure.caption: Fraser & Heitler (1991), Fig. 10(A–C). Residual motor EPSPs at 20°C, 7°C, and with cadmium.

transcript: Slides 34 and 35 separate electrical and chemical components with cadmium and cooling; the steps involved in each type of transmission explain why these manipulations work.
Chemical transmission has many steps that take time.
A presynaptic spike must open calcium channels, calcium must trigger vesicle fusion, transmitter must diffuse across the cleft and bind receptors, and those receptors must open their channels.
Each step slows at lower temperature, so the total delay grows noticeably on cooling.
Electrical transmission is a direct current path.
Current spreads through gap-junction channels as soon as a voltage difference exists, so there is essentially no delay to lengthen.
On cooling, the electrical component therefore stays aligned with the presynaptic spike while the chemical component drifts later, as on slide 35.
Two independent signatures strengthen the conclusion.
Cadmium targets calcium entry, the first step of chemical release, so it removes chemical but not electrical transmission.
Fraser and Heitler describe their result as the first physiological evidence for chemical output from a crayfish giant fiber.
refs: K. Fraser; W. J. Heitler (1991). Photoinactivation of the crayfish segmental giant neuron reveals a direct giant-fiber to fast-flexor connection with a chemical component. Journal of Neuroscience 11(1):59–71. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.11-01-00059.1991

new_slides.title: MG integrates several inputs before it commits to escape
body: Unlike LG, MG rarely fires in a restrained preparation from sensory nerve stimulation alone. Swierzbinski and Herberholz report that MG reaches threshold when subthreshold antenna II input coincides with input from the contralateral MG, or when serotonin is added, so its firing depends on combinations of signals.

MG also integrates several sensory modalities, including touch to the head and approaching visual objects, and it contributes to predator escape, aggression and risk-taking decisions. A neuron that weighs several sources suits a decision that depends on context, not on one stimulus.

A threat ahead of the animal can often be seen before it arrives. A higher requirement for converging input plausibly allows MG to reserve its fast backward escape for threats that several cues confirm.

figure.caption: Swierzbinski & Herberholz (2018), Fig. 1(B). Antenna II-evoked connective activity and intracellular MG potentials.

transcript: Slide 36 notes that most single antenna II stimuli left MG subthreshold; Swierzbinski and Herberholz place that observation in the context of how MG differs from LG.
MG needs combined input.
Previous work cited by the authors brought MG to threshold by combining antenna II input with input from the contralateral MG, or by adding serotonin.
Sensory nerve stimulation alone, which readily fires LG in comparable preparations, rarely fires MG.
MG serves more context-dependent behavior.
The authors chose MG for its greater complexity, including multimodal sensory integration and relevance to predator escape, aggression, decision-making and risk-taking.
In the free animals on slide 8, both a touch to the head and a fast-looming object could recruit MG.
The difference fits the different threats.
A sudden touch at the tail allows no time for evaluation, and LG fires readily.

An object in front can be assessed through several senses, and a stricter requirement for converging input would reduce unnecessary escapes; this functional reading is an interpretation, not a tested result.
refs: M. E. Swierzbinski; J. Herberholz (2018). Effects of ethanol on sensory inputs to the medial giant interneurons of crayfish. Frontiers in Physiology 9:448. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00448
J. J. Wine; F. B. Krasne (1972). The Organization of Escape Behaviour in the Crayfish. Journal of Experimental Biology 56(1):1–18. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.56.1.1

extra_figures.caption: Swierzbinski & Herberholz (2018), Fig. 1(A). Published anatomical arrangement of antenna II input and the MG neuron.

new_slides.title: Early ethanol effects disinhibit escape before sedation
body: Ethanol acts on several transmitter systems and produces biphasic effects in many animals: initial hyperexcitability and disinhibition, then incoordination and sedation. In crayfish placed in ethanol, early intoxication included spontaneous tail flips without any threat.

An enhanced early MG potential fits that early phase, since a larger sensory potential brings the escape neuron closer to threshold. The concentration used, 100 mM, is well above the roughly 17 mM matching the United States legal driving limit, though within the range used in alcohol research.

The enhancement outlasted an hour of saline washout. The authors suggest strong binding to postsynaptic receptors or sustained facilitation of the synapses producing the early potential; how ethanol raises the potential remains unknown.

figure.caption: Swierzbinski & Herberholz (2018), Fig. 3. MG potential amplitudes before, during, and after ethanol exposure.

transcript: Slide 38 reports a larger early MG potential under ethanol; the behavioral pharmacology of alcohol described in the paper's introduction explains why an escape neuron is a good place to look for its early effects.
Alcohol's effects change over time.
Swierzbinski and Herberholz describe alcohol as producing initial hyperexcitability followed by motor incoordination and sedation, a pattern conserved across many invertebrates.
Lower doses produce disinhibition, while higher doses produce incoordination and reduced activity.
The escape circuit reflects the early phase.
Intoxicated crayfish showed increased activity, including spontaneous tail flips in the absence of threat, before activity declined.
A larger sensory potential in an escape neuron offers a cellular correlate of that heightened responsiveness.
Dose matters for interpretation.

The 100 mM concentration exceeds blood levels that impair humans; the authors point out that concentrations in the normal biological range are often insufficient to evoke neurophysiological responses in many preparations.
The saline control on slide 37 rules out simple drift as the source of the increase.
refs: M. E. Swierzbinski; J. Herberholz (2018). Effects of ethanol on sensory inputs to the medial giant interneurons of crayfish. Frontiers in Physiology 9:448. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00448

paper_numbers.17: Swierzbinski & Herberholz 2018, discussion: US legal driving limit

new_slides.title: Pretreatment tests whether two drugs share a target
body: If two treatments act through the same target, applying one first can **occlude** the other: the target is already occupied or altered, so the second adds little. If they act through different targets, their effects should combine. Giving ethanol after muscimol applies this logic to the MG pathway.

Ethanol interacts with GABA receptors in many systems, and muscimol activates ionotropic GABA receptors directly. After muscimol, ethanol no longer produced its clear enhancement, consistent with the two treatments converging on GABA-related signaling in this pathway.

Occlusion is consistent with a shared mechanism but does not prove it. Muscimol's own effects changed the state of the preparation, so ethanol acted from a different starting point than in the ethanol-alone experiment, and either explanation can produce a missing response.

figure.caption: Swierzbinski & Herberholz (2018), Fig. 5. MG responses to muscimol followed by ethanol.

transcript: Slide 41 reports that ethanol given after muscimol behaved differently from ethanol alone; the design is an occlusion test, a standard way to ask whether two treatments share a mechanism.
Occlusion relies on saturation.
If a target is already strongly engaged by the first treatment, a second treatment acting on the same target has little room to produce further change.
If the second treatment acts elsewhere, its effect should appear on top of the first.
The GABA connection motivated the test.
Swierzbinski and Herberholz focused on the GABAergic system because interactions between alcohol and GABA receptors have been described in many animal systems.
Picrotoxin on slide 39 and muscimol on slide 40 probed inhibitory signaling in the MG pathway from opposite directions.
The interpretation has an alternative.
Muscimol alone produced a delayed suppression during washout, so the preparation that received ethanol was already changing.
A shared target and an altered baseline state predict the same missing enhancement, and the experiment cannot fully separate them.
refs: M. E. Swierzbinski; J. Herberholz (2018). Effects of ethanol on sensory inputs to the medial giant interneurons of crayfish. Frontiers in Physiology 9:448. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00448

new_slides.title: Manganese brightens images where calcium channels opened
body: Manganese ions resemble calcium closely enough to pass through the voltage-gated calcium channels that open when a neuron is depolarized, so active neurons take up more of them. Manganese is also carried along axons and slowly across synapses, and it clears slowly, so it accumulates where and downstream of where activity occurred.

Manganese shortens the T1 relaxation time of nearby water, which makes tissue containing it brighter in T1-weighted images. The image records how much manganese accumulated over the stimulation period, not the moment-to-moment firing of neurons.

Accumulation favors regions active repeatedly, which is why the escape protocol delivered many shocks before imaging. Transport across synapses and uptake by every active neuron also mean that bright regions include cells beyond the stimulated pathway, which the unstimulated control helps to bound.

figure.caption: Herberholz et al. (2011), Fig. 3(A,B). Axial brain sections after antenna II stimulation and manganese injection.

transcript: Slides 42 to 44 use manganese-enhanced imaging to mark regions engaged by stimulation; the physics and cell biology of manganese explain both what the images can show and their limits.
Manganese is a calcium analog.
Herberholz and colleagues describe manganese as a calcium analog that accumulates inside cells after passing through calcium channels opened by depolarization.
Cells that open these channels more often during stimulation therefore take up more manganese.
Contrast comes from a magnetic property.
Manganese is paramagnetic and shortens the T1 relaxation time of the tissue that absorbs it, producing a bright signal in T1-weighted images.
The T2-weighted images on slide 43 emphasize different tissue properties, which is why they showed anatomy clearly but the side difference less discretely.
Transport complicates interpretation.
Manganese entering active neurons is transported along axons and, more slowly, across synapses to the following neurons.
The authors point out that all active neurons take up manganese, so distinguishing the stimulated ensemble requires comparisons such as the unstimulated animal.
